question.value: What are the incidence, properties, and evolutionary sequence of substructures in the brightest massive protoplanetary discs in the Ophiuchus star-forming region at 3-5 au resolution?

evidence.quote: Understanding the origin and evolution of substructures in protoplanetary discs and their implications for planet formation is currently one the main challenges in the field.

To better understand the incidence and properties of disc substructures in any given molecular cloud, here we present 1.3 mm/230 GHz continuum ALMA long-baseline observations at 3-5 au resolution of the 10 brightest targets
The ODISEA long-baseline targets were observed during ALMA Cycle 6 under program 2018.1.00028.S, in Band-6 (1.3 mm/230 GHz) and with maximum baselines ranging from 12.6 to 16.2 km.

findings_qualitative.value: Gaps and rings are the most common substructures, with 26 narrow rings and gaps identified across 8 of the 10 ODISEA long-baseline sources.

evidence.quote: By number, gaps and rings are the most common types of substructures. We identify a total of 26 narrow rings and gaps (width/radius $\lesssim$ 1) distributed in 8 sources

findings_qualitative.value: Two embedded Flat Spectrum sources (WLY 2-63 and ISO-Oph 37) lack clear gaps and rings, whereas the Class I object ISO-Oph 54 and all 12 Class II discs in the combined sample show rich substructures, suggesting substructures develop during the embedded stage.

evidence.quote: Two discs (WLY 2-63 and ISO-Oph 37) around embedded protostars with Flat Spectrum SEDs lack the clear gaps and rings that are ubiquitous in more evolved sources with Class II SEDs.

Since other embedded sources in the literature also lack clear gaps and rings, this suggests that these substructures typically appear in the embedded stage of YSOs (age $\lesssim$ 1.0 Myr), but are not necessarily present from the formation of the disc.

findings_qualitative.value: Five discs with large (> 20 au) dust cavities show radial profiles consistent with dust trapping at planet-induced pressure bumps; three (DoAr 44, WSB 82, EM* SR 24S) have unresolved inner dust discs and outer plateaus, while two (ISO-Oph 2A, RX J1633.9-2442) lack detected inner discs and have narrow outer rings.

evidence.quote: The five Objects with large ($>$ 20 au) dust cavities (ISO-Oph 2A; EM\* SR 24S, DoAr 44, RXJ1633.9-2442, and WSB 82) exhibit different degrees of dust accumulation at the edges of their cavities, in agreement with numerical simulations of pressure bumps produced by giant planets.
The other 2 objects with large dust cavities (ISO-Oph 2A and RXJ1633.9-2442) have outer discs with ring-like morphologies and lack ALMA-detected inner dust discs.

claims.hypothesis: Narrow gaps and rings are already ubiquitous from the earliest embedded protostellar stages or emerge during the embedded-to-Class II transition.
claims.experiment: Imaged 10 bright Ophiuchus discs (1 Class I, 2 Flat Spectrum, 7 Class II) at 3-5 au resolution with ALMA Band 6 continuum and combined them with 5 Class II DSHARP discs in Ophiuchus.
claims.result: Only 1/3 (33%) of the embedded (Class I/FS) discs (ISO-Oph 54) show clear gaps and rings, while 2/3 (WLY 2-63 and ISO-Oph 37) show only inflection points; 12/12 (100%) of Class II discs show clear gaps, rings, or cavities.
claims.finding: Substructures typically appear during the embedded stage of YSOs (age <= 1.0 Myr) rather than being present from disc formation, and become ubiquitous by the Class II stage.

evidence.loc: Towards an evolutionary sequence of substructures in massive discs
evidence.quote: We find that only 33$\%$ (1/3) of the embedded (Class I/FS) sources show deep gaps and bright rings (i.e, ISO-Oph 54), while 100$\%$ (12/12) of the Class II objects present such features.

Since other embedded sources in the literature also lack clear gaps and rings, this suggests that these substructures typically appear in the embedded stage of YSOs (age $\lesssim$ 1.0 Myr), but are not necessarily present from the formation of the disc.

claims.hypothesis: Large dust cavities (r > 20 au) in massive accreting transition discs are carved by giant planets that create pressure bumps trapping mm-sized dust grains, rather than by photoevaporation.
claims.experiment: Measured radial brightness profiles and central-beam inner disc fluxes of 5 large-cavity discs (DoAr 44, WSB 82, EM* SR 24S, ISO-Oph 2A, RX J1633.9-2442) and compared them to numerical dust evolution models with an embedded 1 M_JUP planet at 0.5 and 5 Myr.
claims.result: All 5 profiles peak near the cavity edges; 3 systems (DoAr 44, WSB 82, EM* SR 24S) have unresolved inner dust discs (0.04-0.1 M_earth) and outer plateaus matching younger (0.5 Myr) model snapshots, while 2 (ISO-Oph 2A, RX J1633.9-2442) lack inner dust discs and show narrow rings matching evolved (5 Myr) snapshots.
claims.finding: The radial profiles and inner dust disc detections strongly support planet-induced pressure bumps and dust evolution, and rule out photoevaporation.

evidence.quote: The five Objects with large ($>$ 20 au) dust cavities (ISO-Oph 2A; EM\* SR 24S, DoAr 44, RXJ1633.9-2442, and WSB 82) exhibit different degrees of dust accumulation at the edges of their cavities, in agreement with numerical simulations of pressure bumps produced by giant planets.

Three of the five objects mentioned above (EM\* SR  24S, DoAr 44, and WSB 82) have small inner dust discs detected by ALMA, which strengthen the evidence for a planetary origin of the cavities and rules out the photoevaporation mechanism.

claims.hypothesis: The diversity of substructures across massive protoplanetary discs in Ophiuchus represents an evolutionary sequence driven by giant planet formation and radial dust drift.
claims.experiment: Constructed a flux-limited sample (F_1.3mm > 70 mJy, 15 discs representing the brightest 5% of Ophiuchus discs) spanning Class I, Flat Spectrum, Class II full, pre-transition, and transition SEDs, and analyzed their substructure morphologies.
claims.result: Morphologies progress from smooth discs with inflection points (embedded FS), to concentric narrow gaps and rings (Class I and Class II full), to large cavities with inner discs and outer plateaus (Class II PTD/full), to large cavities with narrow outer rings and depleted inner dust discs (PTD/TD).
claims.finding: A tentative evolutionary sequence is proposed in which planet cores carve narrow gaps, grow via runaway gas accretion into gas giants that carve wide cavities and filter dust at pressure bumps, leading to inner disc dust depletion and outer ring narrowing.

evidence.loc: Towards an evolutionary sequence of substructures in massive discs
evidence.quote: The scenario discussed above should be considered a tentative hypothesis at this point, but it represents a coherent picture of the evolution of substructures in discs that can be tested by detailed numerical modeling of each "evolutionary step" (e.g., see Sec. 4.2.2) and future observations.

We combine our ODISEA long-baseline sample with the brightest Ophiuchus objects observed by DSHARP to create a flux-limited sample (F$_{1.3mm} >$ 70 mJy) and construct a putative evolutionary sequence in which the substructures observed in massive protoplanetary discs are mostly the result of planet formation and dust evolution.

why_this_data.value: Selected the 10 brightest ODISEA discs (>70 mJy) not in DSHARP to build a complete flux-limited sample of the brightest 5% of discs in a single star-forming region at 3-5 au resolution, spanning Class I to Class II evolutionary stages.

evidence.quote: To better understand the incidence and properties of disc substructures in any given molecular cloud, here we present 1.3 mm/230 GHz continuum ALMA long-baseline observations at 3-5 au resolution of the 10 brightest targets of the "Ophiuchus DIsc Survey Employing ALMA" (ODISEA) project
The DSHARP project observed a total of 20 discs in several star forming regions, but their sample was restricted to Class II sources and also excluded “transition” discs with known dust cavities.

why_this_method.value: Processed long-baseline data alone (except WSB 82) because combining with 0.2'' data degraded resolution without adding features; used Frankenstein visibility fitting in addition to CLEAN to test sensitivity of substructures to beam convolution.

evidence.quote: We have also produced images combining the long-baseline data with the snapshot ODISEA observations at 0.2$''$ resolution from Cycle-4 (PID = 2016.1.00545.S). However, we find that this degrades the resolution and does not improve the image quality or provides additional results.

In order investigate how the properties of the substructures we derive depend on the data processing, in Appendix 6 we use the python module Frankenstein (frank, (cite: jennings2020)) to produce model images (Figs. 11 and 12) and a new set of radial profiles.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Combining Cycle-6 long-baseline data with Cycle-4 0.2'' resolution data for all targets (rejected for 9 of 10 sources because it degraded angular resolution without improving image quality)

evidence.quote: We have also produced images combining the long-baseline data with the snapshot ODISEA observations at 0.2$''$ resolution from Cycle-4 (PID = 2016.1.00545.S). However, we find that this degrades the resolution and does not improve the image quality or provides additional results.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Photoevaporation and dead zone models for large transition disc cavities (rejected for the massive accreting discs in this sample due to detected inner dust discs and radial profile shapes)

evidence.loc: Discs with large inner holes and their connection to disc evolution and planet formation
evidence.quote: (cite: pinilla2019) compared their models to multi-frequency ALMA data of EM\* SR 24S at 0.1$''$ (11 au) resolution and concluded that the observed brightness profiles were most consistent with a planet-induced inner hole and inconsistent with photoevaporation and dead zone models.

Three of the five objects mentioned above (EM\* SR  24S, DoAr 44, and WSB 82) have small inner dust discs detected by ALMA, which strengthen the evidence for a planetary origin of the cavities and rules out the photoevaporation mechanism.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Condensation fronts (snowlines), magnetic dead zones, self-induced dust traps, and secular gravitational instabilities as alternative origins for narrow gaps and rings

evidence.loc: The possible origins of gaps and rings
evidence.quote: Examples of proposed mechanisms include condensation fronts (cite: Zhang2015), self-induced dust traps (cite: Gonzalez2015), magnetic dead zones (cite: flock2015) and secular dust instabilities (cite: takahashi2014; loren-Aguilar2015).

limitations_admitted.value: Pre-main-sequence stellar masses and ages are model-dependent and photospheric properties of embedded sources are very uncertain.

evidence.quote: The masses and ages of low-mass pre-main-sequence stars are model-dependent and notoriously difficult to derive ((cite: baraffe2002; soderblomPPVI)).

limitations_admitted.value: Dust opacities at mm wavelengths are highly uncertain, and assuming T = 20 K and optically thin emission for inner discs may overestimate their mass by T/20 K or underestimate it if optically thick.

evidence.quote: However, dust opacities at mm wavelengths depend on grain size distribution, composition, and structure and still remain highly uncertain.

evidence.loc: Discs with large (r > 20 au) dust inner cavities
evidence.quote: we warn the reader that this might overestimate the dust mass in a warm inner disc and that the real dust masses can be lower by factors of T/20K. Alternatively, the mass of the inner disc could be underestimated if the emission is optically thick.

limitations_admitted.value: Feature characterization is limited by wavelength-dependent grain size sensitivity, ALMA beam convolution (making features appear wider and shallower), distance uncertainties (1% to 20%), and the assumption of a single center, PA, and inclination across each disc.

evidence.quote: Second, all the features are convolved with the synthesized ALMA beam, which can make deep and narrow features look wider and shallower than they really are.

Third, the sizes and locations of the features all scale with the distance to the objects, which have uncertainties ranging from $\sim$1$\%$ for targets with accurate Gaia parallaxes to $\sim$20$\%$ for objects without such information.
Namely, we assume that all features in a given disc have the same center, position, angle and inclination.

limitations_admitted.value: Frankenstein models assume azimuthal symmetry (failing on asymmetric features in ISO-Oph 2A) and do not reproduce the inner cavity of ISO-Oph 196, whose inner disc morphology depends on CLEAN details.

evidence.quote: Since the Frank models assume azimuthal symmetry, the models necessarily fail to identify the azimuthal structures present in the ISO-Oph 2A disc.

Frank also fails to reproduce the cavity we find in the CLEANed images of ISO-Oph 196, but it finds an infection point close to the center of the disc instead. Further tests on the object reveal that the morphology of the inner disc is dependent on the details of the CLEANing process.

limitations_admitted.value: Comparison between observed radial brightness profiles and numerical dust evolution models in Fig. 9 is purely qualitative (linear intensity vs. log surface density, without radiative transfer or fine-tuning).

evidence.loc: Discs with large inner holes and their connection to disc evolution and planet formation
evidence.quote: We note that Fig. 9 compares observations in linear scale to model results in logarithmic scale and should only be considered qualitatively, not only for the reasons mentioned above (the lack of any fine-tuning and radiative transfer)

referee_caveats_inferred: The sample of embedded sources (1 Class I, 2 Flat Spectrum) is too small (N=3) to draw statistically robust conclusions about when gaps and rings first emerge.

High 1.3 mm continuum optical depth in the inner ~25 au of massive embedded discs like WLY 2-63 and ISO-Oph 37 could hide existing surface density gaps rather than indicating an evolutionary absence of planets.
Visual identification of gaps, rings, and especially inflection points from 1D radial profiles is subjective without a formal significance threshold or parametric model fit.

missing_for_reproduction: Self-calibration solution intervals (solint) and SNR cutoffs for each of the two phase-only iterations
TCLEAN cell size, image size, deconvolver, and stopping criteria, plus the manual CLEAN masks
Exact uv-range or Fourier annulus definitions used when fitting disc centers, inclinations, and position angles
Frankenstein configuration parameters (e.g., alpha, w_smooth, R_max, N)
reproducibility.estimated_data_volume_inferred: ~50-150 GB (12 long-baseline execution blocks in 2018.1.00028.S with 3 TDM SPWs and 1 FDM SPW, plus snapshot execution blocks from 2016.1.00545.S)
reproducibility.score_reason: Raw data and project codes are public, CASA and pipeline versions are explicitly stated, and visibility/profile analysis recipes and equations are clearly described and tabulated; minor deductions for missing self-calibration solints, TCLEAN cell/mask parameters, and frank hyperparameters.
reproducibility.rediscovery_reason: All ALMA data are public under 2018.1.00028.S and 2016.1.00545.S, the imaging and radial profile analysis steps are straightforward to replicate, and the paper provides extensive numeric tables of disc geometry, fluxes, dust masses, and substructure locations/depths/widths.

Methodology for extracting deprojected radial brightness profiles and defining gap/ring locations, widths, and depths
Frankenstein (frank) non-parametric Gaussian process code for reconstructing 1D radial brightness profiles directly from visibilities
Numerical dust evolution and planet-disc interaction models compared with transition disc radial profiles
